utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Case Number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Mr. Oric, are you follow the proceedings in a language you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours, gentlemen. Yes, I can follow the proceedings completely in a language I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour, my name is Jan Wubben, lead counsel for the Prosecution, together with Mr. Gramsci Di Fazio, Ms. Joanne Richardson, and our acting case manager, Ms. Djurdja Mirkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you and your team. Appearances for Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. I am Vasvija Vidovic. Together with Mr. John Jones we are representing Mr. Naser Oric. And we have with us our case manager, Ms. Jasmina Cosic, and our CaseMap manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Good morning to you and your team. Any preliminaries? Can we bring in the witness? The sooner we finish the better.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to everybody on behalf of Slavoljub Zikic. Good morning, gentlemen. Good morning, everybody, on behalf of Zikic, Slavoljub.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Zikic. You may sit down. We are going to start the cross-examination today. May I just remind you that you are testifying under oath and that you have an obligation and responsibility to answer the questions that Mr. Jones will be putting to you truthfully, honestly, and fully. Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Zikic, I'm going to be asking you questions today and many of those questions will require only a yes or no or I don't know answer. And if I pause, it may be for the interpretation, so don't necessarily feel you have to add anything with this pause. Now, I don't know if you can see me, I'm over here, in case you're wondering where this voice is coming from. Now, I'm going to start by taking you back to happier times. You told us a nice story on Tuesday how Muslim forces in Zanjevo, which is also known as Abdulici, would help you before the war by farming the land for you while you would sit and smoke. Do you remember telling us about that story? And that was because you didn't know about farming.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. That's how it was and the way I described it, and I affirm that again today.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Can you give us the names of --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the counsel speak into the microphone for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's a problem with the lectern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Perhaps you can do it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Can you give us the names of those two or three people who helped you farm your land.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why not? For example, Husnija Hasanovic [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Any others?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sabrija Selimovic and his sons.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And these people were good friends then at that time?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. Real friends. At that time we weren't thinking about who was a Serb or who was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And these were friends for many years?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have land right in the middle in Zanjevo or Abdulici. That village has two names. That was always that way. My parents had an ox cart in that area. They would go up there and they would move around or travel around in the village until they finished all of their business there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You know Zanjevo very well, I take it. It's right also, isn't it, that you were in this area, Fakovici, Zanjevo, throughout May 1992 doing your job as manager of the post office. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1993 the post office was not --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I said 1992; apparently it's been translated as 1993. May 1992, you were there the whole time?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992 we began to sow the corn. When we finished with the sowing -- but already in May around late May when you start to cultivate the corn, this was in Zanjevo or Abdulici, we were not able to cultivate the corn. We could only do the parts that were quite close to Fakovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Isn't it right that in May 1992 the Muslim farmers you referred to could no longer help you with your land because they had to leave Zanjevo, they had been expelled from Zanjevo?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In May they were not expelled, but everyone was already aware in some way that there was some kind of mistrust that was beginning to appear; that's how I understood it. They left -- or they were expelled, whatever you like -- from Zanjevo in the month of June. I can't remember the date. I remember just that it was Serbian holiday, St. Jeremiah's day. They were picked up by buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We can continue. I was going to ask you to keep your answers short, but that's a helpful detail. They were picked up by buses or taken away from Zanjevo?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Buses were provided and this commander, Jovanovic, Slavko Jovanovic, went there to tell him that he could not guarantee for them, that he didn't know what would happen to them tomorrow. We have buses. You have your own free territory in Kladanj. You can go to the school -- or you can come to the school. I don't know at what time they were supposed to all gather together. The buses will leave then and you will have a safe journey towards Kladanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's right, isn't it, Mr. Zikic, that these people were forced to leave, because why would they leave their homes and their land and their livestock that they've cultivated for so many years?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I can tell you for sure, at that point in time, on that day, they were not forced to leave but it was sufficient that the commander, Slavko Jovanovic, was not able to guarantee what would happen the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's a form of threat, isn't it? That was a form of threat, for him to say he couldn't guarantee their safety.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can draw your own conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Isn't it right also when they left their homes were burnt, the homes of the Muslims in Zanjevo?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Is it also right that the Muslims in Zanjevo, like many farmers in the area, grew crops and kept livestock. But they -- after they had left kept trying to come back to reap the harvest that they sowed because they had no food. Is that something you're aware of?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since they had already moved out, they would come to get their food but during the night. We would see lights going through the woods and we didn't react to that. They would be taking their own food during Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond the night at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You say you didn't react to that, but isn't it right that Serb village guards or soldiers or whatever you want to call them would shoot at people moving around at night and people died in that way?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of a single case like that, believe me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You mentioned yesterday mines. You referred to a boar that had been killed by stepping on a mine. Isn't it right the area was mined precisely to prevent people from coming back and getting their food?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mines were placed in such a stupid way, both on the Muslim side and the Serb side. There was no record of where the mines were placed. There were no sketches, so that Serbs would trip on their own mines as well as the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to move to another area, and you'll forgive me if I move around a bit. I'm going to go to and fro a little bit today. I want to take you to the 5th of October, briefly, 1992. You've described events in the village on that day. The fact is, isn't it, that you don't know who started the shooting in fact. In fact your wife thought at first that it was your soldiers firing in the area. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First I would like to correct you. It's not the 1st of October but the 5th of October. I was gathering the corn and when the firing started, the shooting, I said to my wife that we should stop and see what was going on. And she thought, well, no, it's probably our people who had too much to drink. Then we went up higher from where you can see all the villages below.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You don't need to recount your whole story. I'm asking very specific questions and just a yes or no will do most of the time. My question is: You don't know how or why the actions started on the 5th of October, do you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How could I know that?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And on that day you were with your wife Milenka and your sister-in-law Vera Vesic, weren't you? The name of the sister-in-law is Vera Vesic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is true. There were only the three of us in that field.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: These are fields in Fakovici rather than the ones in Zanjevo you mentioned earlier?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were gathering the corn in the field that I have in Fakovici. We didn't go up to the other fields to gather the corn. When I say "up there," I'm thinking of Zanjevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And when you were led off later by the people who took you captive, you were led along a river to Poznanovici, if I understand correctly. And I would be grateful if you would tell us the name of that river.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The village itself was called Mlecva, so officially it was called the Mlecvanska River.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now I'm going to deal with your captivity in a moment. But first briefly I want to ask you about events after your release. Now, in a statement which you gave to the Prosecutor you said that after the exchange we were taken to the Serb forces command headquarters. I was debriefed. My statement was taped and transcribed. The man who debriefed me is dead. My question is: Do you remember this you were debriefed by the Serb forces command headquarters after you were exchanged?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And that was very shortly after you were exchanged, a day or two perhaps?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And in that debriefing, the people interviewing you were very keen to find out who was responsible for your detention and mistreatment, weren't they? That's why they were debriefing you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand how I should answer to this. I think they wanted to see what we -- how we were treated in prison, what happened to us. I stayed there for a short time. As I said yesterday, my relatives came to pick me up immediately. I'm not there on the footage that you saw here yesterday, either.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: But when you were debriefed, how long did this last roughly, can you remember? An hour?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. I don't know. I was still unfit to think about those things at that time. I just wanted to cross over into Serbia; that's where my children were. I wanted to see them and I wanted them to see me. I didn't think about anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: But isn't it right that you had been through a very unpleasant experience, probably one of the most unpleasant experiences of your life, and so that when you were interviewed you were very keen to say what had happened to you and to name anyone who you thought was responsible for your mistreatment. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I didn't know anyone up there, just Mr. Naser Oric and I knew Akif from before. I can't say that we were really -- that we knew each other very well, but we knew each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Isn't it right in that statement you never mentioned Naser Oric when you were first debriefed?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true. They asked how -- what was the conduct of Naser Oric and Akif Husic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: They put the question to you about Naser Oric? Or did you volunteer the name Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. I know that there was talk about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We'll come back to that in a moment. You told us yesterday that you never before the war set eyes on Naser Oric but the reason you concluded it was him was purely and simply the person said he was Naser Oric. And if you'll permit me, I'll read back your remarks. You were asked: "Now, could you tell us how you knew you were talking to Naser Oric?" You replied: "That's what he told us, that he was Naser Oric." And then in your 2000 statement to the Prosecutor, and I'm referring to page 5, ERN 00538907, you said: "I knew it was Naser Oric because he would say to us Have you heard of Naser Oric and he would say to us when we said yes that I am he, I am Naser Oric." It's right isn't it, that that's all you had to go on? Someone saying I am Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So the person that said I am Oric was simply lying or playing some joke or quite simply pretending to be something he wasn't, that's something you would not have known at the time, would you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could -- I had four prisoners who were there when I got there and when he appeared at the door they said "Naser Oric."

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's new, isn't it? You didn't tell us that before.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I couldn't recall every single detail. But as soon as he came in, they said "Naser." They didn't say Oric, and I had heard earlier that his last name is Oric.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Isn't it possible that they were basing themselves on the same information as you, namely that this person had said I am Naser Oric to them?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Let's just deal with what you know, never mind the other prisoners. Isn't it correct that if I had come to the prison at that time and I had said, I am Naser Oric, you would have left the prison saying I met Naser Oric. He had receding hair. And you would have described what you and I talked about. But in fact you would have been describing a person who said they were Oric and not actually the person who was Oric. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably, if you introduced yourself that way and I didn't know the other man, I would probably believe your story.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Precisely. Now, the fact is -- well, let me put it this way. According to what you said in your 2000 statement, this person announced that he was Naser Oric in a somewhat theatrical manner. He said, I am he, I am Naser Oric. Is that how you recall it, him saying it in a slightly pompous manner?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand. Do you want me to describe him or something like that?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, I'm trying to establish the character of this person who spoke to you. I'll come at it a different way. Do you know that this person, whoever he was, told you at least one lie, didn't he, about killing Arkan, as we know Arkan didn't die for years later? I mean, if you're aware of that.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, maybe he was boasting or something like that, at least that's what I can conclude.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Exactly. I mean, you know -- you're aware that Arkan didn't die until years later, in fact in 2000. Is that correct? You're aware of that now?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the specific year. I know that he was killed in Belgrade. I read it in the papers.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: After the war. That he was killed after the war?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, long after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, if I want to take this slowly because it's important. You said yesterday about your conversations with the person you called Mr. Naser. I'm going to quote from the transcript. "He came about four times if I count all the conversations. Perhaps I will remember the last conversation and then I can remember the second-to-last. He came with a pistol to that hall or corridor and he asked me personally: Do you know whose pistol this is? I said, Mr. Naser, you're the one holding it. It must be yours. He said, Well yes, right now it is. But do you think who it belonged to yesterday? I said, well, there's no way for me to know this, I've been in prison for some time." Just pausing there, you'd only been in prison for a few days at a point, hadn't you? In total you were there for 11 days. So you had been in prison for a few days at that point rather than a long time.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was imprisoned on the 5th of October and I was exchanged on the 16th. It's up to you to count the days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I would only ask if counsel will be quoting from the transcript he will give a page and line number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are right. Thank you, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I will provide that. I am basing myself on the LiveNote electronic version and it was 11.35.17.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: To continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: "I said: Have you ever heard of Arkan? And I said yes. He said What do you know about him? I said, I know he's rich, he's married to a popular singer called Ceca. Something along these lines. There was no way I could have known anything more than that at that time. He said This is his pistol. Zvornik fell yesterday and has been in Serbian hands. He said, Zvornik fell yesterday and this is the pistol that I used to kill Arkan. I said, war is war." I'll just wait for the transcript to catch up. That's what you said yesterday. And I'm referring to your 2000 statement. The reference is 00938907, page 5, a similar conversation: "One time he," Oric, "had a nickel-plated pistol and he asked us on a visit to the cell if he ever heard of Arkan and we said yes. He then told us This pistol is Arkan's and he was killed yesterday and now it's mine." So a number of questions about that. Firstly, and it's a perhaps a minor detail, but the story has changed already a little, hasn't it, between your 2000 statement and what you told us here. Because now you're saying the person who claimed to be Oric said he killed Arkan with the pistol, whereas before he said that Arkan had been killed and he now had his pistol.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that statement. Even if I had heard he had been killed, I don't remember that. I don't think I ever gave such a statement nor did I ever hear anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, we'll come back to that. But leaving that detail aside, this was the first lie, wasn't it, that Arkan had been killed? Because as you told us he survived the war. But isn't it also a lie Zvornik had fallen, because in fact the Serbs captured Zvornik in the early stages of the war and never lost it. So that was another lie which this person told you, wasn't it, about Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, I don't think you understand me sufficiently then. I did not say that Arkan was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No. Mr. Zikic, it hasn't been put to you that you said Arkan has been killed. What I'm putting to you that this person who spoke to you has told you at least two lies, according to this conversation he had. He lied when he said that Arkan had been killed and he lied when he said Zvornik had fallen. That's what I'm putting to you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said a while ago, I think he was just being boastful, but I didn't believe that he had actually done it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, that's why you may understand now why I was asking you if he was pompous or theatrical. Isn't it right that this person was a bit of a joker and he told you these two lies in your first conversation with him? In other words, this person was telling you one lie after another.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The four visits I remember. Once he --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... we'll come back to the four visits because I want to ask you questions about each visit. I want to stick with this conversation. There's something else wrong with what you told us yesterday about this conversation, isn't there? You said you applied to Mr. Naser. He said, have you ever heard of Arkan? And I said, yes. And he said, what do you know about him? I said, I know he's rich. He's married to a popular singer called Ceca. Arkan didn't marry Ceca until more than two years later, didn't he? In fact it's on the 19th of February, 1995, if you're aware of that.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I know, at least based on other people's accounts, is that she had been married to a rich man from Asia, apparently, an oil tycoon or something like that. And at the time he had in some way liberated her, perhaps even earlier, for a couple of years and he took her. Now, when exactly they were married I don't know because precisely I didn't attend their wedding, if you see my point.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a couple of exhibits we downloaded from the Internet concerning when Arkan married Ceca and when he died. They're not in Bosnian so I obviously can't present them to the witness. It may be a matter for judicial notice; it may be a matter which we can deal with in some other way. I don't intend to pursue it further with this witness apart than to put questions to him in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, you can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Mr. Zikic, what I'm putting to you and I hope you understand this. Arkan was not married to Ceca at that stage. And this conversation which you say took place quite simply could not have taken place was Arkan was not married to Ceca and you, as you say, didn't attend their wedding and presumably didn't have a view of the future. So this conversation is something you've invented or imagined based on events that occurred later. Isn't that what happened? You're embellishing your account of your captivity by telling imaginary stories of imaginary conversations with Mr. Naser.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. And these thing being said about Ceca and Arkan or when they got married, my understanding was they were married at that time. I heard stories that people told perhaps even as long as two or three years before the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's fine. I was only going to object to the lengthiness of the question. And if counsel could keep his questions a bit briefer, I think it would be easier for everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think the Trial Chamber has weighed this witness enough to know whether he is being harassed, whether he is being asked a fair question which he can take and answer. I think he is a very strong personality. He can --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He can answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Is it for the Prosecution to monitor the length of my questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's why I didn't hear her objection or what she had to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Proceed, but you do have an inclination to put long questions which with something for his age may be a little confusing and for the interpreters difficult to follow. If you can reduce them or bring them down in -- yes, Ms. Richards.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'll do my best, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Mr. Zikic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before you proceed on something else, do you want these exhibited or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, Mr. Siller, please. The first one which was a single page with the title "who killed Arkan"

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, it gets the exhibit D132.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Will be D132. The other one consisting of two pages and title of "turbo nationalism" reporting on Arkan's wedding, three pages, will become D133. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And my suggestion to you, Mr. Zikic, and you're free to agree or disagree, is that every time you speak of these events you give a different account of the encounters with the person you say was Naser Oric. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We'll speak about that in a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, there was -- I apologise to Mr. Jones for interrupting you like this. You know it's not in our style. But my attention is being drawn that when we indexed the previous two documents, put them -- brought them into record and gave them a number and I said the first one of which is D132, and I said it consists of a one-page document with the title "Who killed Arkan?" I was only given at the time one page, when in actual fact the document consisted of two pages. The previous page I mentioned of "who killed Arkan?" Is the second page of what will be D132. But D132 consists of two pages, the first one being a page with the title "Arkan: Death of an warlord: Special Report" showing a number of people gathered around the grave or the tomb where allegedly Arkan was buried. So these two pages will form document D132. Thank you and sorry for the mistake. And you may proceed and make -- again, I apologise for interrupting you in the process of your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, the description you gave of the person you said was Naser you gave in your 2000 statement, I'm referring to ERN 00938907, page 5, was: "Naser was well-built, 180 centimetres tall. Handsome man. He wore no beard." Is that correct? Is that how you remember this person?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything is correct but I did not say that he wore a beard. It looked more like a regularly unshaven man to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it must be a question of interpretation. They must have --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Isn't it right that your description was that he didn't have a beard or that he did have a beard?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again I must say it is possible that I gave such a statement, but what it really looked like, when I said a beard I didn't mean like an Orthodox priest or a scientist or someone like that. It was a very, very short beard, just mere stubble. So I'm not sure I should call it a beard at all. Maybe he just hadn't shaved for a long time. I don't think he was really trying to grow a beard. That's now how it struck me at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Again I think there's a problem with translation. Perhaps the witness could be shown a copy of his statement which could solve the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which statement are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's the one of the 25th of March, 2000. And in the English I'm looking to page 5 -- well, I've given the reference already. I'd like the witness to be shown.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And if you look at page 5 and it's 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 -- 6th paragraph. And it's the first sentence. In English we have "Naser was well-built, 180 centimetres tall, handsome man." Sixth paragraph, first sentence. And in your language it's [B/C/S spoken]. Is that a correct description?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that moment, yes. But in as far as I was able to judge after all the beatings I had received, well that's a different matter altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: My point to you is this: The description of that person is of a pretty average person, isn't it? Average height, handsome, well-built is a matter of opinion. There wasn't anything distinctive of this person, was there, that you noticed?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing distinctive. And he treated us fairly, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, in terms of the visits paid by this person to the prison. In this statement while you still have it in front of you, you state, and I'll refer to the English. It's page 5, 00938907, third paragraph. "He would come to the building every morning." And you were there for 11 days, so that would be 11 visits. Yesterday you recalled four specific occasions and conversations. Correct me if I'm wrong about that. The first conversation in which he asked you about Fakovici and the people there; the second occasion which I think you said what happened on that occasion; the third conversation he asked you, are you bloody; and the fourth conversation about Arkan. Can you let us know which is correct? Was it every day or was it on four occasions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment before you answer the question. Because at the end of the same paragraph you have been reading from where it describes Naser Oric, well-built, 180. At the end the last sentence of that paragraph is "during my stay in that prison, I think Naser visited the cell every other morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, that contradicts what's on the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You should put this to him as well. Because in the statement we have got two statements. One says every day; the other one says every other day.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I was going to, Your Honour, but it gets rather complicated to put all these contradictions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It was one of the questions I was going to put myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I think it's easier if the witness just lets us know was it every day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that was going to be my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. As I said, That was one of the questions I had prepared.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We can expect progress. I'm wondering if the Prosecution is going to be popping up every five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's divide the question into three parts. Mr. Zikic -- Ms. Richardson, please. Mr. Zikic, in this statement you gave to the Prosecution in the year 2000, you are reported as saying that Mr. Oric, Mr. Naser Oric, the man you described as Naser Oric, sometimes you say he used to come every day. At another part of the statement you say he used to come every other day. Which is the correct of the two? Was he coming there every day or every other day? One day yes and one day no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think someone probably misunderstood. Either it was you yesterday or the statement was not taken correctly. My statement then as now is that he came every day to the building in which we were being held. And then suddenly there would be discipline. As to the visits to the prison itself, it is the four times that I mentioned, not 11 visits to the prison itself. But throughout those 11 days we knew in the morning when Mr. Naser Oric came to the building. A deadly silence would descend. Whereas, during the night when he was away people would be drinking and singing and shooting into the air, or what have you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So your evidence is that from the 5th of October to the 16th of October every day Naser Oric visited the prison and you knew of this because of this air of discipline that descended over the building, if I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Didn't it strike you as strange that this person, if he really was the military commander of the armed forces was at the prison every day rather than at the front lines? Was that something that made you suspect that this person wasn't a military commander?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think this is something for me to conclude. He could have had deputies or assistants, if you are talking about the army on the front line. Whether he went or not, I really don't know. We knew and those people who were in prison had told me before, Naser is a disciplined person. Well, if he's a disciplined person, then the soldiers, too, would have been disciplined. At about 7.00 in the morning certainly what I can say is the atmosphere changed in relation to how it would have been in the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: My suggestion to you, and perhaps it isn't something you can help us with, is that this person was more of a prison governor being mistaken for Naser Oric, and that's why he came to the prison every day. That's not something you can help us with and I'll move on. I want to deal with prior statements you made. Do you recall making a statement in August 1994, to an investigative judge in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes -- no, not the investigating judge. I think it was someone from The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, there's a statement that you gave to people in The Hague which I will deal with subsequently. But what I want to ask you is in 1994 you spoke to Serbs, people from your area, about these events and gave a statement. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Someone did come over to see me, but whether it was on behalf of the SUP, on behalf of the army, or on behalf of a third party, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Where did they come to see you, where were you when they spoke to you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They came to see me at my home. A man came. I have no idea who he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your home in Fakovici or somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fakovici, yes. I don't remember that I travelled anywhere else. I did give interviews also to some international TV stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If we could -- I think it's been distributed, perhaps, the statement from 1994 or it will be distributed. I'll give the references for the record. In English it's L0044700 to L0044710. In Bosnian it's 0065244 to 00652412 [sic]. And if that could be shown to the witness -- if it could be shown to the witness and his signature or what purports to be his signature could be shown. If the witness could look at that. If he could look at his signature as well or what purports to be his signature as well. I'm going to draw his attention to certain details in this statement. If you could have a look, Mr. Zikic.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which signature?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: At the bottom of the page. Is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, it's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And isn't it right that this statement, if you look through it, has certain details that you've told us about here, for example, that the Muslims said [indiscernible] was our Milosevic, on page 4 of the English. The story about the dog which you told us on page 8, and the rather odd story which obviously stuck in your memory about the old man and the young girl and smoking a pipe of tobacco and that since she is immature we Serbs are immature, too. That story on page 8. So that's your story. What is in front of you is a statement which you gave and signed, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And you signed it after being informed that you would -- to tell the truth and that you mustn't conceal anything. Isn't that right? I want to read part of that statement. I want to refer you to part of the statement where you discuss Naser Oric. And in the English it's pages 6 to 7, L004705 to L004706. And it starts off, the bit I'm going to read: "During these interrogations, the commander of Muslim forces in Srebrenica, Naser Oric, used to visit the room. I did not know him then but he somehow knew a lot about me." I'm pausing there. Do you remember saying and is that true?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He addressed me as Upravnika, manager.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. He's not, as far as you know, from the Fakovici area, is he, Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you thinking of Naser, Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, the person who you say is Naser Oric and who seemed to know a lot about you, he's not from the Fakovici area, is he, or someone you recognised as a local?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Would you have any idea why he would know a lot about you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's something that I would like to know, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: But carrying on, "he, Naser Oric, asked me" -- I'm just moving down a little bit, down the page -- "whether I knew why they attacked us on 5 October, on Monday, on a usual day, not on some Orthodox holiday as it was usually conveyed. When I answered that I did noted know why they had done so, he explained that there was an information about an inspection in Fakovici performed by Akif, performed on 2, 3, 4 October and took an order from a file giving it to me to read. I remember the contents of that order quite well and I can quote it in its completeness 'pursuant to the inspection of Fakovici on 2, 3, and 4 October, I hereby order to attack Fakovici on 5 October, Monday, at 1200 hours" -- looks like 25.000 -- "2.500 well-armed soldiers on the front line 8.5 kilometres long. Naser." Now, my question to you is: Is that really right, that after two years after these events when you said you were disorientated and confused, you remembered word for word an order which Naser Oric allegedly read out to you? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether I said Naser in that statement. That was about Mirzat or from Mirzat. I'm not sure how that was interpreted. I'm not sure if I mentioned Naser Oric. I would not say something that wasn't like that. I think this was when Mirzat was interrogated me on behalf of the army. It was not at Naser Oric's.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: My question is this: When you were interviewed in August 1994, is it right that then, two years after -- nearly two years after these events, that you remembered verbatim an order which had been read out to you? Or did someone insert this in your statement, is what I'm driving at.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't inserted. When I was asked about all sorts of things, this was with Mirzat. Do you know why we attacked on that specific day; why we attacked Fakovici on that specific day; of course I didn't know. If I had known I would have been on the other side of the Drina. I wouldn't have waited to go through what I had to go through.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You say he then took a document from a file, gave it to you to read, and you then memorised the whole contents of that order in those moments you had it in front of you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A wrong interpretation again. I do not mention Naser Oric there but Akif Husic. Yes, Akif Husic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: My question is a very simple one. Did you maintain in the interview in 1994 that you had memorised word for word an order which had been given to you to look at and you were then able to reproduce that order word for word? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether I repeated it word for word. Maybe it wasn't like that. But if I gave a statement, I gave it based on my recollection. I cannot see the original. I don't know whether it states that in the statement or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Let's just go back a statement. You said this is not something which Naser Oric said and yet it's right, isn't it, that you signed this statement in which it said that Oric said this to you. You signed that as the truth, and in fact it wasn't true.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: See, I did not say ever -- I did sign it, but I don't know if I read it back or if it was read back to me. I don't know. But we're talking about Akif Husic here and not Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes -- just for the record, Mr. Jones, sorry to interrupt you, but I think this is important for -- I'm sure you know it. The -- basically the last sentence of that statement precisely ends with the following words: "The protocol has been loudly dictated. It contains everything I stated. I do not wish to read it. I recognise it as mine and accordingly sign it."

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes and every page is signed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He didn't read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: But it was read to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what it says, it was read to him. Again, using the same basis of suppositions here and suppositions there, they may have read something different to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, the conclusions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly, the conclusions are what we have here and we will draw our own conclusions. Yes, Judge Eser would like to put a question. One moment, Judge Eser.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: I have a question as to the English language. If you say "the protocol has been loudly dictated. It contains everything I stated." Now, there's a difference between who dictated it, whether the witness dictated it or whether somebody else dictated it --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: My understanding --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: There may be a difference between the dictation and then what was written down.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I understood it to be "loudly dictated" probably has been read out loud. That seemed to be the most likely interpretation. Your Honours, there are a number of inferences which one could be drawn about this statement. I've pointed to passages which reflect this witness's testimony. As Your Honours have observed, it's a matter for you to draw conclusions about whether this witness has adopted it as his own based on a number of factors and not purely if and how it was read to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: I just wanted to ask because the German understanding of dictated -- we have the same word in German -- dictated would not mean it was read to the person interviewed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: My colleague might be able to throw some light on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And this is what it says -- this is precisely what it says in the Serbian -- the Serbo-Croat version because you have [B/C/S spoken] in the beginning of the sentence before [B/C/S spoken]. Yes, Ms. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Your Honours, perhaps I can clarify the procedure because we might come up with that in the future. What is usual in the course of conducting an investigation in the course of our criminal proceedings is that the investigative judge asks the witness a question, the witness answers, and then the judge dictates loudly for the record in the presence of the witness. And this is then stated at the end of this statement. So the investigative judge dictates aloud what the witness says and then this is signed at the end by the person who took the dictation or the record and then by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, what Madam Vidovic has stated may be the case sometimes. But in fact these statements the way they were taken may not comport with what was just said by Madam Vidovic. I think these statements were taken in a different manner back in 1994. Today the witness may give the information to the investigative judge and it's read back, and that may be the procedure today. But in 1994 that was not the procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's try and cut this short because I think we are wasting time. Mr. Zikic, this gentleman who came to see you in August 1994, this Serbian gentleman and interviewed you, at the end of which you signed this document. Was -- first of all, did he have a tape recorder? Did he have a typewriter? Was he jotting down himself? Or did he have someone else writing down what you were saying? Let's take them one by one. Did he have a tape recorder?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did he have someone helping him or was he just by himself, alone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I gave so many statements in different places, so I cannot remember who came and who they were with and when they came.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, Vaso Eric is going to be a witness, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Was he carrying a typewriter, he or someone else, or a computer or a portable computer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think that he was. I don't know. I cannot remember that detail and I could not say whether he was carrying it or not. I really don't recall that detail. I don't even recall that statement, but it exists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but you have seen your signature on it. Do you have reason to doubt the authenticity of your signature or do you confirm to us that it is indeed your signature? Does he still have it, Usher?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is my signature, but I do not recall whether it was read back to me or not. It is my signature, though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you remember whether you signed that document on the same day you were interviewed by this gentleman or whether you signed it days or a period of time later?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I cannot answer that question. I really do not remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you don't remember either whether that person read out to you the statement before you signed it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you remember that person dictating to someone else what needed to be registered, put down, in writing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I said earlier I gave a lot of statements and I cannot remember whether each statement was read back to me or not. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's fair enough and that's the end of it as far as I am concerned. Of course you may proceed with the matter as much as you like, but I don't think you're going to get anywhere, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No. I would simply ask this be made an exhibit, the 1994 statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's have a formal copy of it, because what I have is mine and I may have some notes on it. So this is going to be Defence Exhibit D134. Correct? D134, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, we've spoken of two statements, prior statements, by you today, Mr. Zikic, a statement to The Hague investigators and this statement. Now I want to turn to a third statement which is when you were debriefed on the day of your exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And with the usher's assistance I would ask that the next exhibit, prior statement, be exhibited. And just to explain for the record the English version is ERN 00366735, 00366739. We've received that from the Prosecution under receipt 11, but we found the same version in the report to the UN commission of experts sent by Ambassador Dr. Vladimir Pavicic from the FRY. The Bosnian version has the ERN 00832033 to 0832035, and if it would assist the Court, we also received this with receipt 11 as part of a criminal complaint. It's something I can deal with in the witness's absence, if need be.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Zikic, I would like you to look at that document which has been put in front of you. And it's right, isn't it, that this statement contains, again, a lot of details which you've given in evidence. On the first page that you were with your wife and her sister. You went past the guard post where the people had been killed. I think you'll confirm that was true, wasn't it, on the 5th of October, 1992, you went past the guard post where people had been killed. Can you confirm that, Mr. Zikic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like a specific question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: My specific question was: Can you confirm that on the 5th of October, 1992, you went past the guard post and you saw that people had been killed there. It's a yes no question.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we escaped from the field by the path towards the road to Bratunac and Skelani, that guard post as I described it was actually a house where people were incinerated with a Zolja. It was perhaps 50 to 80 metres from the bank of the Drina. It was a weekend house. We didn't see the dead, but we just recognised the voice of my sister who was moaning and wailing. After that she died, and she was found on the front door of that building.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Turning to the second page in the English we see in English, and if you'll follow if you can in the original, "they tied my hands with rope behind my back and ordered me to guide them along Mlecvanska River. I had no choice. They were afraid that the fields might be fined." I'm sorry -- no, it's in the transcript. "They were afraid that the fields might be mined. I went forward but they did not trust me. They thought I might be ready to kill myself and take them with me". Isn't it right that you told us that you were led along the Mlecvanska River and the other details you see there, Zulfo on the white horse, that the people didn't trust you to lead them through minefields and a further detail that a man said I won't drink from the same bottle as a Serb; all of those details you have confirmed for this court, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: He's about to answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let him answer --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The witness said --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, could you please repeat your answer, Mr. Zikic, before you were interrupted.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said, if understood it properly, they tied me up, they drove me along -- not drove me but they led me up along the river.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zikic. In fact I was asking you to repeat your answer when you said "da" twice. Isn't that right that the last question I put to you, you said yes? In answer to my question you said "yes"?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to have it also for the third time, if the Court permits me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think this is all very confusing to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I make one observation. My colleague was rebuked yesterday for interrupting the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I haven't -- I haven't.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The witness replied yes twice very --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I haven't allowed Ms. Richardson to intervene. In all fairness I think your question is confusing to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: He answered it clearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go through it bit by bit, Mr. Jones because it's not fair.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: What I'll do is I'll ask the witness to look at his statement. I'll ask him that he can confirm that he's told this Court certain details in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Firstly, isn't it right that you were with your wife and her sister on the 5th of October, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was there in the cornfield.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Just a yes or no will suffice, if we're going to get through this. That your hands were tied by rope?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That you were guarded along the Mlecvanska River?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That Zulfo was on a white horse?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That the people guarding you were worried that you might be ready to kill yourself and take them with you by leading them into a minefield?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They placed me at the head of the column, but as we were walking for about a half a kilometre along the river we came to a place where a wild boar was killed. When they saw the fur that was dismembered, I don't know how to describe it. They said they shouldn't permit the Chetnik to lead the column because he will guide us into a minefield and kill himself, too. So that's what happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's an exact repetition of what he told us before.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And that a man said to you, I won't drink from the same bottle as a Serb? You don't have to tell the whole story again. Isn't it right that that's part of your account, that a Muslim said, I won't drink from the same bottle as a Serb?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is 1.000 and not 100 per cent true.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So this is, is it not, your statement or a statement by you about these events, the statement in front of you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I find it hard to read even with my glasses, but you just go ahead please with your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, could this be the first statement you made when you were debriefed on the first -- on the day of your exchange?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which statement you're thinking of.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, the one that is in front of you I'm suggesting that that could be a statement you referred to when you were debriefed on the day of your exchange.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Witness, if you know, you know; if you don't know, you don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know, that's why I wanted to have an explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So leave it at that, please. If you don't know, you don't know. And this is an unsigned and unstamped and undated document which had it been sought to be admitted by the Prosecution you would have certainly objected to, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, may I take exception to that. I've tried, given that it's undated and unsigned, to elicit from this witness that these are details that he's given before and therefore it's not his statement.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please not overlap. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are putting to the witness -- you are putting to the witness that this is his statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And that it is indeed also his very first statement that he made. You are not allowing for the possibility that it isn't even a statement of his.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's perfectly open to this witness to look at the statement and say, ah yes, I recall now, this is a statement I gave on the day of my exchange. That might be possible evidence he could give.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you wishing to tender this document in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this is being tendered in evidence by the Defence and admitted and marked as Defence Exhibit 135. Any further questions to the witness on this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Continuing on page 2 of the statement, if you could look at that it says: "Behind me went the Turk, or call him what you will, an Ustasha, Zulfo by name." Now you told us you were called Vlah, which is an insulting name for Serbs. And isn't it right that calls Turks or Ustashas is just as insulting?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, unfortunately that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Is that the word you used to describe Zulfo when being interviewed?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the moment that I found myself in.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, seeing the word Turk there as a description of Zulfo and saying now that that was the moment I found myself in, does that help you with the question whether this was the first statement you gave when you were still very much caught up in your anger of what had happened to you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Bosnia up until about 20 or 30 years ago the Serbs always referred to Muslims as Turks. After that, they became Muslims. So could you please explain to me how we should now move to Bosniaks? In my life there are three different names for those -- for that ethnic group. Also at one point there were also undeclared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment before you move because he hasn't answered the question obviously. The question was by far completely different. Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, just briefly, I wanted to point out to the Trial Chamber that the witness does not have this statement in front of him and I believe Mr. Jones asked that he look at this statement. So if we could have that shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, that's fair enough. I suggest that you indicate the line -- Usher, please go next to Madam Vidovic and Jones. Could you indicate on the text on this B/C/S the line where the word "Turk" is used.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If the transcript could say that I'm not getting anywhere. I'm doing my best, Your Honour, with an undated statement and I apologise if it's tiring to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you indicate to us as well where the line is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I thought -- it's page 2. 00366736.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, no. On the Serbian text.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's where it says [B/C/S spoken] and it's approximately --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which page? First page.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: 20 lines from the bottom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [B/C/S spoken].

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, let me put the question to him and try. Now, you have an opportunity, Mr. Zikic, to look at these three pages, and on the first page you have also been referred to the word "tutsin [phoen]." Have a look at that document again. Would you agree that this is a transcript of your very first statement -- of the very first statement you made after being exchanged? We are asking you this question because this document does not bear a stamp, does not bear a signature, neither yours nor anyone nor is it dated. So we need your help to know whether we can take this document to be a true transcript of your very first statement after your release or whether we leave it as an undated, unsigned statement. What is your answer to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems to me that we need to clarify two terms, the term "Turk," so as not -- so as anyone would understand that I'm not trying to accuse anybody from the state or the Republic of Turkey because they're Turks as well. This Turk refers to the term that was used for over 500 years and longer, and perhaps to this very day, referring to Muslims. But as far as the statements are concerned, there are several statements so I cannot remember when I gave each statement when it was taken down, written. I really don't know anything about that. But I really want to explain so that the gentleman would not understand me as referring to somebody who was from Turkey who was a part of their forces. This term refers to Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: May I put one further question -- well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course. I was trying to help you, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you remember using the expression and I'm going to say it in your language moja zuca? Does that mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please repeat that?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Moja zuca?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the first time in my life I'm hearing of that word and I don't know what it means.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I may come back to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour I should mention that this was submitted as part of a criminal complaint against Alija Izetbegovic, Sefer Halilovic, and Naser Oric. It's provided by the authorities. It's not a random piece of paper that we've --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm not saying it was a random piece of paper, but before it was admitted in evidence, obviously we could only look at it as three pages unsigned, undated.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm sure Your Honour appreciated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Whatever. Now it's an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It still remains unsigned, undated, and unstamped, but at least we have had some answers to it so we will be in a better position to decide whether to give it any probative value because we admit it now on the face of it, now as it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In light of this witness's testimony and other factors which may come to light.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Especially so, because we may end up with the person who drew this up saying, yes, this was the statement I took from the witness the same day he was exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have passed the 10.30 mark. I wonder if it's convenient for you to have a break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. I do have a few more questions on this exhibit, but a break is fine now. But I should say not making progress I thought it may be and we go with him until tomorrow. This is a very important witness and the Prosecution had him all yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I am not going to stop you. I told you we are not going to curtail either of you when it comes to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Zikic, in spite of technical developments, we are stuck. The transcript is not being put on record and your testimony is important, so we have to wait until the transcript is working. I'm sorry for this. I'm assured it's only going to take a couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It seems to be working now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's see, because I still haven't seen -- yes, it's working now. So, Mr. Jones, sorry for that. I hope it does not -- has not created any frustration to you. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In relation to the last exhibit, the undated statement, we have a new exhibit. And just to explain, it's the cover letter by which that statement, the English version, was submitted to from Frits Kalshoven and it's dated 18 May 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's have a look at it first before we authorise you to proceed with any further questions to the witness. Are you going to question the witness on this document or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No. I just want to tender it to clarify the date of the undated statement. Just to explain, the ERN you have 017954 on the first page. Obviously we haven't copied the whole document but the sequence goes up to 017957 and there's a memorandum of war crimes and genocide in eastern Bosnia, the communes of Bratunac, Skelani and Srebrenica committed against the Serbian population from April 1992 to April 1993. That's dated Belgrade, April 1992. And then we have the statement which I was referring to further along in that same document starting 018061.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: May the Prosecution receive a copy of this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, I am taking it for granted that you are receiving a copy.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Where -- you just said that this is dated Belgrade 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The cover page, the very first page is 18th May, 1993, but then the memorandum which I referred to says Belgrade, April 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Because that's why I raise the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Wherever I saw a date it said 19th May, 1993, and I wonder if I was missing something. There is -- okay. You are tendering this?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, of course. So one moment, Judge Eser. This will be Defence Exhibit 136. Judge Eser.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Now, the Defence Exhibit 135 had the English version and the Bosnian/Serb version. Now, was the Serb version also included in this letter to Kalshoven or do you know anything about the genesis of the Serb version? Was it the original and then translated into English or visa versa?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I believe the -- I'll wait for the interpretation. Yes. I believe the Serb version was not attached in the document sent to Mr. Kalshoven. We received it as part of a criminal complaint, as I mentioned earlier, against possibly -- the B/C/S version in a criminal complaint against Izetbegovic, Halilovic, and Oric, and that's -- we have that document. And the ERN for that criminal report is 00632970, for the record. And perhaps I should tender that as well. One moment, please. It might be useful for me to provide that also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Obviously I'm not going to tell you what to do and what not to do, but I'll agree with you that that is useful.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'll tender that. I just have one copy of that for now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The registry will attend to that, will have copies made. And this will be Defence Exhibit D137.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, just a few more questions, Mr. Zikic, on this document and I am going to ask you to look again at it if you could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, we have got a different idea, Mr. Jones. I think before you ask further questions to this witness on this document, we are going to provide it -- provide him with it again and we are giving him all the time he requires to read it completely from beginning to end. And then you may go ahead with all the questions that you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's an excellent suggestion, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, Mr. Zikic, look at me, please. You have been shown this document before, before the break, and you have been asked questions about it. I'm giving it back to you. It's not a long document; it's only two and a half pages or even less than that. Could you be kind enough to read it all. And when you've -- not aloud, read it for yourself -- and when you've read it just let me know that you've finished reading it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In order not to take up any more time, this is indeed my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And in addition to that, do you have any idea when you could have made this statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I've given so many statements, I can't even remember how many.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which brings us back to square one, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: He's adopted it as his statement at least now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Just two final questions on this statement. You told us earlier, and I put it to you in your statement to The Hague investigators, that when you were debriefed your statement was taped and transcribed. That's the statement when you were debriefed on the day of your exchange. Now, do you recall whether that statement was signed by you, the which was transcribed on the day of your exchange or not?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember well, my family came to pick me up immediately and I didn't attend the interview at all. I'm not even in the footage that was shown. My brother-in-law came and he took me to his home so that I could have a bath and be sent to see a doctor. If I remember correctly. God knows I really can't vouch for anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: But isn't it right you referred to a statement which was taped and transcribed. So my question is: That statement, is it right that you didn't sign it, the statement taken from you on the day of your release?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you've looked at that statement. Isn't it right that although you discussed your captivity in Srebrenica and you refer to people like Akif, that nowhere, nowhere in that statement do you mention Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned Naser Oric in the remaining statements except for those visits up there, and I always stated that he treated us, the prisoners, in a fair manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, but I'm just sticking with your -- the document in front of you. And it's right, isn't it, that nowhere in that statement is there any mention of Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't quite finish reading it, but I do believe that I did mention him. If you've gone through the statement and you see that that is indeed the case, then it must be the case I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I don't know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, the only objection I have at this time it's being asked of the witness whether or not he signed a statement taken from -- as he was debriefed. And now we're on -- the way counsel is phrasing the question as "that statement." I think the record should be clear that this statement that he's being shown now, there's -- the witness has not said that this is the same statement that he did not sign or otherwise. So I just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
