utterances.text: Point taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We were not taking either Mr. Jones or Mr. Zikic agreeing that this is indeed the first statement. I mean, there's no agreement as of yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We know it's before April 1993. And I was referring to the 2000 statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It always begs the question if it was the very first statement, which would have been in October, November of 1992 and the request to or, the document sent to Mr. Kalshoven.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: My point obviously, Your Honour, is this is the very first statement we have. That it was sent from Mr. Kalshoven in May 1993 and the others date from 1994 and 2000. So I'm putting to the statement that in the first statement we have there's no mention of Naser Oric. I don't know if it's necessary for him to see his statement to agree with me on that point. I think Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think his reply is sufficient and the document is there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the document is there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And I put it finally to you, Mr. Zikic, isn't the reason you never mention Oric is that you never saw Oric in the prison? This is a fantasy, an invention, that you've come up with since.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I came back from prison I was in such a condition that I was not even able to find my way back home let alone give a reliable statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You also told us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But you haven't answered the question. It has been put to you, Mr. Zikic, that when you finally decided to specifically mention Naser Oric, it was not because you had really met a man who told you he was Naser Oric four times but because you were inventing this. Mr. Jones is suggesting to you that this was an invention. It's not the truth. You never met anyone called Naser Oric, that you just invented this. Do you agree that you invented this or are you saying the truth when you repeat it on more than one occasion that someone had met you and told you he was Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. You may chose to believe it or to disbelieve it. But no one came to seem me since it happened, therefore I cannot prepare myself for this testimony. I thought it would only be in relation to my time in the prison. No one ever instructed me or visited me. Unfortunately they didn't even come over to see what my house is like, therefore what do you expect now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But do you confirm that when you said that you were -- you met someone who described himself as Naser Oric, you were telling the truth? Or was -- or were you just inventing this story? This is what Mr. Jones is asking you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not invent this story because those other people who were in the prison already knew him and they said, Stand up, Naser is coming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The conversation about Ceca being married to Arkan is an invention, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He has answered that question. You put it to him before and he answered it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Another point. Yesterday you also told us that Naser Oric asked you if you knew Uros Bogdanovic and Bozidar Kovacevic. Now, that's not in any of your prior statements, is it, that conversation? Alleged conversation. That's not something you've never told anyone before -- I shouldn't say anyone. It's not in your prior statements, is it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I forgot the last name you mentioned, but it's about Uros Jovanovic who was captured before I was captured. He had been beaten. And before they exchanged he asked me if I knew anything about him, what had become of him. I said I heard he had been sent on to Bratunac and then sent on to Belgrade and that he died as a result of the beating and I said this because he is my neighbour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Hold it. I don't want you to repeat this story again. The question that Mr. Jones -- I'm trying to help you, sorry, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: At not at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're putting questions and you're not getting the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm obliged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He pointed out to you that here in that chair where you're sitting you've told us that Naser Oric or the man who described himself as Naser Oric asked you something about Uros Jovanovic. This is what you told us here, but Mr. Jones is pointing out to you that in the other statements that you gave before you came here, statements which we have here, you never mentioned this before. And he is asking you to agree or not to agree that you had never mentioned this fact before in any of your statements while you are mentioning it now. Do you agree that you never mentioned it before to anyone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I disagree. I may have forgotten this, but I do know that this is the truth, what I said before.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: My suggestion to you, and I won't pursue it, but I will put it one more time is that each time you recount these events about your captivity, you add new conversations, new events involving Naser Oric, and that you're fantasizing about these conversations which never happened. I know you probably won't agree with me, but that's the suggestion I'm putting to you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones is suggesting as we go along and you mention new things, basically these things are not the fruit of recollection of what's happening but just the fruit of imagination, of your imagination. Do you agree with him or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I disagree. It cannot be about my imagination because back in those times --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Enough. Next question, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm moving to a new area all together.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you were asked yesterday the following question and I'll refer to 12.55.21 of the transcript. You were asked: "I'd like to ask you some questions about the injuries you received while you were in prison in Srebrenica. Could you tell us what type of injuries you received in the beatings." That was the question. You replied: "I have medical certificates. I had two broken ribs, one possibly fractured." But it's not true, is it, that your ribs were broken in detention. They were broken when you were first arrested in Fakovici. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The statement that I gave says that one rib was broken in Fakovici when they tied up my hands. As for the rest, I didn't even know when the other ribs were fractured until I was released from prison. I didn't even know that they were broken at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... just you need to be accurate about when you sustained which injuries. And I'd like to refer you, it may not be necessary to put it in front of the witness, to your 2000 statement ERN 00938905, page 3, third paragraph. It's written: "Immediately after that another soldier ran to me and struck me on my ribs, on my left side with the butt of his rifle, broke two of my ribs," and this is referring to the moment of your arrest. I'll carry on: "This was confirmed later by an examination done by a medical doctor in Lazarevac, FRY." So that's why I wanted to clarify the question you gave yesterday that your ribs weren't broken in the prison; that damage was done long before in Fakovici. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't think it's a yes or no question. I don't know when my ribs were broken. I didn't even know. The first night I had severe pain --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and my conclusion was that the ribs had been fractured.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: But isn't that right that that first injury to your ribs on the day of your arrest was done by a dark man, somebody you suggest as being dark, possibly a Gypsy?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The man that I believed to be a dark man, I think that was my statement, didn't hit me; it wasn't him. Rather, he came up to me and he carried a knife and he instead of saying "Chetnik" said "Chelnik," which means the leader. And then Zulfo shouted no or someone else from that group at any rate was saying, There's still a lot of time before we get to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. But it was around that time when you describe someone as a soldier struck you on your ribs with a rifle butt, breaking your ribs.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I'm saying is I felt pain on one side. The next morning I couldn't even cough. I suffered severe pain, which means I was injured at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You say that Zulfo, the person you called Zulfo, stopped you from being injured further on that occasion. My question is: Isn't it correct that these were violent times, this was war; it was a time when an engaged person could kill a Serb in a moment of anger and vice versa. That's something which was quite common at that time?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but we are talking about white people.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, but my question to you is: Isn't it right that Zulfo may have saved your life on that day when the dark person approached you with a knife?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was thanks to him that you see me here today.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction. The witness did not say a white man or white people, he said "Beli" which may be a reference to a person's name.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We might be skipping ahead there, then, because isn't it right, Mr. Zikic, that you didn't see Beli until you arrived in Srebrenica? Just a simple yes or no, Mr. Zikic. You didn't see Beli on the day you were arrested in Fakovici, did you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, sticking with the 5th of October, you mentioned Zulfo, but Zulfo didn't take you all the way to Srebrenica, did he? He -- or you came to be with another group of people who took you there?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was about 1 kilometre further down the road behind us that I saw Zulfo in the column and I never set eyes on him again until we arrived in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. But -- so Zulfo didn't escort you to Srebrenica, did he?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Actually, I didn't see him. I don't know whether he was moving behind me or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the people who took you there you mentioned took you on the van or truck, and in fact they didn't mistreat you, did they? In fact they were worried about your hands losing circulation. Again, Mr. Zikic, you don't need to give a lengthy answer. Is that right, that they didn't mistreat you in the truck?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I got onto the truck that was waiting, we were moving away from Fakovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm not sure if there's a problem with interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know either, but he's certainly not -- there is no relation between question and answer. I suggest that you put the question again and I'm sorry, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No problem at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The people on the truck didn't mistreat you, did they?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And they were concerned when they saw that your hands were blue because they had been tied.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not the men on the truck, but rather when I came outside the prison the man who untied my hands said, Your hands are all black. Why didn't you complain? Then someone from the group said, Why are you feeling sorry for this Chetnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, staying with your injuries -- and I'm sorry to have to ask you about it, but I do -- you told us yesterday how you were not able to raise your right arm above a certain height, but that injury was accused by Beli after you had left the prison, wasn't it? It didn't happen in the prison, that particular injury?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My arm was not injured in the prison but on the truck. They stopped the truck. He said, This is farewell to you now, and then he hit me on my right shoulder with his rifle butt.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And that was on the 16th of October, on the day of your exchange?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And isn't it also the case that when you were exchanged, that locals in the area of Potocari came out and attacked not just you but the other men as well because they were angry that Akif Ustic and his men had been killed in an ambush?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So you're saying you weren't mistreated in any way around Potocari by locals on the day of your exchange?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not apart from some children who were there waiting. Our truck was waiting for the exchange to take place and then some children climbed on board, but I don't think that really matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: But isn't that right that the major fractures you suffered occurred before and after you were in the prison and not while you were actually in the prison in Srebrenica? And by that I'm referring to your rib injury and your arm injury.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is your conclusion. I don't think I could make that conclusion myself. We were beaten in the prison. As for the injuries, I do not know the extent of these specific injuries until an x-ray was made in Lazarevac later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. You told us yesterday when you were seen in prison that it was obvious that you had been beaten. I asked you a moment ago about whether these were violent times. Isn't it right that someone who saw you at that time with blood on your face wouldn't necessarily know when or where it had happened, if it happened before you arrived in the prison?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How could something be before?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You told us you were beaten before you arrived in the prison.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That happened on the way. From Fakovici towards Poznanovici they beat me and Zulfo said on one occasion, Don't be playing heroes over an old man; you have others to be heroes before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's, let's, let's bring it to -- when you arrived in the prison on the 5th of October, after that long journey, did you have a bloody face? Were you covered in blood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How can I know that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you a little bit about the other four people who were in prison with you. And you've described, I think, that they were black and blue; and in fact I think you said you were all, all five of you, more dead than alive. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That morning when I arrived they were so exhausted and bloodied that I really felt panicky.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I was referring, actually, to the very end when you were exchanged, presumably at which time you would all be in an even worse condition, on the 16th of October. Mr. Zikic, I see you're getting ready to give a long answer. My question is simply: On the 16th of October, is it right that the five of you were, in your phrase, more dead than alive, in a very bad state?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's also what others said about us.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'd like to replay a section of the video we saw yesterday and it concerns the third --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The one you object being admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, we were very clear that we had no objection to the segment with Radic, because he's going to be a witness. That segment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course. You still insist on your motion, after seeing the limited use that the Prosecution made of that video yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I understand they intend to use it with the next witness, so we need to preserve our position. If everyone has that on their screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not yet. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If we could play a little bit of that. We don't need the sound.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Mr. Zikic, do you agree that Mr. Radic, at least there, he's certainly slightly emaciated, but he doesn't seem to have any bruises or injuries on his face. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree that I do not see any because in the morning we were told that wash off everything, down to the last drop of blood from ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm not talking about blood, Mr. Zikic. I asked you about bruises or injuries on his face, and there don't appear to be any, do there, at least from this clip? Is that someone who you would really describe as more dead than alive?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Upon orders of Beli to beat me, he couldn't even get up so that he could beat me. But he had to and he did that. But Beli was not satisfied with that and made him hit me harder. But he wasn't able to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: My question was about his injuries, but I'm going to move on to another question, and we can stop the video. You told us that Zoran Brankovic on the 16th of October went immediately to hospital because of his injuries. My question is: Isn't that -- wasn't that to be treated for injuries he sustained after he left the prison when he, as you described, was taken off the truck and attacked by four people. Isn't that why he had to go to hospital?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that when we returned I told you that three or four people grabbed him and smashed him against the concrete, and that's when the blood rushed out and that's when he was injured the most.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Precisely. And that was after you left the prison on the 16th of October, wasn't it? You were outside the prison at that stage.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we set out towards Bratunac, they took us back again and took us all off the truck. And then again when we were going into the truck to go for the exchange, this happened. So it happened in front of the prison building.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It was outside, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: This happened outside, in the open air?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In front of the prison, not inside, not in the cell.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, neither you nor Mr. Sarac nor Nevenko had injuries that were so bad that you had to go straight to hospital, did you, on the 16th of October, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course we did. You saw Nevenko at least, on the photograph. You saw what he looked like.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, but you mentioned that Zoran had to go straight to hospital because of his injuries. But isn't that right that Sarac and Nevenko were fit enough to be interviewed by the people interviewing them, and didn't go straight to hospital on the 16th of the October?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you know when they went to hospital, if they did go to hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've said several times already that I was picked up right away and they stayed behind. I was told that Zoran was sent to the hospital. That's what I was told by all of these people who went to see, the citizens. I was picked up right away and I'm not in the footage or photographs or anywhere. So I don't know what happened with them afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's right, isn't it, that you went to your home on the 18th of October, 1992, before you went to hospital?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had to go there before. How could I get to the hospital if I didn't go home before?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's right, isn't it, that you didn't go see a doctor until the 19th of the October, 1992, three days after your exchange?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remained behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If we could look at the medical report which was tendered yesterday by the -- I believe it was tendered by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's P464.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It doesn't need to be shown to the witness necessarily, but let's -- looking at that report it's written: "Patient was in a detention camp in Bosnia, he was beaten on several occasions. OBJ." I'm not sure what that is in English. "Multiple contusions of the face and head, front of the abdomen and ribcage, on the back and lower back, RTG fracture of the tenth left rib, suspected fracture of the eleventh rib." So there's confirmed fracture for one rib. But then "TH" which I assume is therapy -- "Therapy: Rest and checkup in two weeks." But isn't it right when you saw the doctor then three days after your exchange he told you you needed to rest and you should come back in two weeks for a checkup?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 21 days. But I didn't go back to the checkup because the same person told me there is no therapy for that, I can just give you Brufen for your pain and you have to take care not to use too much of it because it's not good for your stomach. So I didn't go ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. I just want to be clear then. You didn't need to go to hospital, you didn't go to a hospital for any extended period of time after that, did you? You were released and you stayed at home?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just went for an examination. I had the x-ray and I was told to report back in 21 days. When I came home an elderly woman came to see me. She said, He doesn't need to see a doctor; just give him some sheepskins and he can change them every 24 hours and then he doesn't need to go. And then I got nine sheepskins and I changed them every 48 hours. That helped me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you able to tell us which doctor treated you? Because I'm afraid we don't see it on the copy. We may need to ask for the original. But can you help us with the doctor you saw and where they are based?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw that doctor on that one occasion and never again, because like I said I didn't go back for the checkup.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We may need to pursue the original of that, but that needn't detain us now. You also said yesterday that you lost weight. Do you know how much weight you lost when you told us you were detained for 11 days and you never went to the toilet?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is true. To this very day, I have the same problems. And I had to go and see a doctor because of that the day before yesterday. As far as my weight is concerned, I wasn't really paying attention to my life. I didn't check that. If I had known what would be happening to me later, perhaps I wouldn't have even gone to see the doctor at all and come what may.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us yesterday of your reunion with your wife and how tearful that was. And you started to tell us how your brother-in-law brought you to the house in Bratunac and your wife said, Budimir, have you gone crazy as well? And he replied, Drago is on the stairs, please stay calm. And correct me if I'm wrong, weren't you actually about to tell more of a joyful story about your reunion with your wife because she thought you were dead? That was the story you were about to tell us, unless I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, this is not my wife; this is my sister-in-law. In the meantime I had been buried. The guardhouse that I'm talking about was incinerated by Zolja, so you didn't know who was in there. My sister was in the cornfield with the hostess of that house who is a younger woman. My sister was wounded, and she set out towards this house where these guards were. She was killed on the threshold.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Zikic, it was merely to clarify that when you told this story that the tears which were shed were also of joy that you were alive, not horror at your appearance. That's what I want to be clear about. Because they thought you were dead -- you had died. That's all, Mr. Zikic. You needn't give a lengthy answer.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The wife, when she came into the house, in the house of my uncle's -- my cousin, she looked at me and she didn't even approach me at that moment but she sat down on a chair and she kept looking at me. Only later did she approach me and come up to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we could tender the next exhibit. It was actually the document which was attached behind the medical report. It throws light on what this witness was saying how there had been a funeral service for him, but I don't intend to ask any questions about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. This will be D137 -- 138. 138.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Zikic, I'm just going to ask you a couple more questions about this period of your detention, then I'm going to go back to an earlier period in 1992. So just so you know it's only two or three more questions on this subject. The first is this: Is it right, then, that you were not present when Sarac and the others were interviewed, as we saw on the videotape? You weren't present for that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you told us that someone called -- who you think was called Kukic died in the prison. You never saw him, did you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They told me about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You don't know personally how he died, do you, apart from what you were told? Sticking with what you know yourself.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally don't know anything. I know about it on the basis of stories told to me by those who were in the prison. This was something that happened before I arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And it's right, isn't it, that you didn't see any killings of anyone when you were in the prison?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Just one moment. I answered with a "no," but I didn't actually see anyone.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch everything the witness said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not see anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. So now I'm going to move to a new area --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have another half an hour before we have the next recess.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I would suggest that you use it now and we will go on recess -- on break at 12.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Perfect. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You finish when you finish. We're not going to cut you short or curtail on your time, the time you need to finish with this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So I'm going to go back now to early 1992 and Fakovici and the situation there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Maybe it calls for an explanation but I think all in all it doesn't, but once it has been brought to my attention I will go through it. In answering your last question the interpreters could not catch everything that the witness was saying. He was about -- he was being asked: "It is right, isn't it, that you didn't see any killings of anyone when you were in the prison?" And he started saying: "Just a moment, I answered with a no, but I didn't actually see anyone." What did you mean to tell us exactly?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I what I wanted to say was that I did not see anyone with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But did you hear of any killings inside the prison?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: He answered that yesterday and I didn't wish to revisit that subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes., Mr. Jones, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You told us how you were mobilised in 1992 and how the Serbs in Fakovici were issued with uniforms and weapons. And you said how this was distributed out of a warehouse or storage space which was located in the school. Correct me if I get any of these details wrong. So the weapons and the ammunition was in the school in Fakovici; that's where they were stored?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And you were actually in charge of issuing weapons and ammunition, weren't you, so you have a good idea of the quantities of weapons and ammunition which were stored there?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there only at the beginning, and yesterday I was explaining why I was exchanged. At that time there were very few weapons. I tried to explain. The first thing that I saw when I got there were some old type of weapons, but these weapons were using 7.62-ammunition which is also used for pistols.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Can you just help us with the dates there. When did you arrive and when did you leave the depot or the warehouse, however you wish to describe it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know the date. I wasn't really paying attention to it. Perhaps it was in late May that I took over the depot.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: When did you -- did you remain at the depot until the 5th of October, 1992, or did you leave before then?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. I said, since I had to go to Bratunac to pick up the mail twice a week, I asked the director in Bratunac to ask the command to relieve me of this duty because I had to go to Bratunac twice a week and distribute everything, pensions and social assistance was arriving. It had to be distributed. So then they fulfilled my request because I didn't want to be at the depot.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And when was that that they fulfilled your request, roughly?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that this was in late July or early August. There was no need for me to remember something like that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's fine. But isn't it right that in terms of the ammunition, weapons in the school, there was a lot of ammunition, and by that I mean thousand -- more than a thousand 7.62-millimetre bullets, as well as hand grenades. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time that I was at the depot there weren't any, but I don't know about the period when I left.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You did tell us yesterday that you were issuing ammunition, 7.62-millimetre and other weapons. Correct me if that's wrong. You did issue weapons and ammunition to people?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you please repeat the very end, please. I didn't hear it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You issued weapons and ammunition to locals in Fakovici, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So you have at least an approximate knowledge of the quantities of weapons and ammunition which was in the school, don't you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. But up until July. October is quite some time later.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We'll come back to that. This was organised by the komandir Slavko Jovanovic, who was a local SDS leader, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Was Batko Markovic also involved in the distribution of weapons?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand "distribution."

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, weapons being received in your depot and then issued to locals. Did you come across Batko Markovic in that capacity?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bato [as interpreted] Markovic had nothing to do with the depot and he didn't hang around the depot at least. For as long as I was there he never entered it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, let's stay with Slavko Jovanovic. Isn't it right that since he was an SDS leader that the SDS was involved in distributing weapons to the local Serb population in Fakovici?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if there is one, then somebody must have been involved, but I cannot say whether that was so. I cannot say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, I'm looking at your 2000 statement, ERN 00938904, third paragraph, and it seems you said: "We had M-48s and semi-automatic rifles known as PAP. The local SDS had given them to the village." Now, do you recall saying that and is that true?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that the SDS was giving it. I think I said that they had M-48s, semi-automatic rifles, and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand that word.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But that was during the time I was in the warehouse. For later, I had no idea about weapons and I didn't go to the warehouse at all. I have been relieved of everything that related to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The essence of it is -- what we want to know is whether you know if the SDS was handing -- was making these weapons available or not; whether, in other words, the SDS was involved in making these weapons available. Because you said so in one of the statements. You said so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that all the parties, the Muslim, the Croat, and the Serbian were included or participated in the arming.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you about the numbers of soldiers in Fakovici, and that's bearing in mind what you told us yesterday, that for you a person with a weapon, whether organised or not, is a soldier. Now, on that definition of yours, how many soldiers would you say were in Fakovici in October 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In October 1992 I think 15 soldiers at the very most, up to 20 armed soldiers. I'm telling you again. That was no sort of army really, because when we say "army," we all know what that means.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Isn't it true that there was in fact an battalion strength unit of the VRS in Fakovici linked to the VRS in Skelani at that time?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Skelani were a bit stronger but as I said, we were cut off from Skelani and Bratunac equally, therefore I can't say anything about either Bratunac or Skelani. All I can tell you is about my so-called local commune of Fakovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And Fakovici, you told us that you issued weapons to people but a lot of people didn't know how to use the weapons. Isn't it right that training was organised, particularly in Ruljevici, precisely so that people would know how to handle these weapons?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that, when that happened. I only had to do with a post office throughout this entire period. I never even travelled anywhere. I don't know about Ruljevici. It's in a different area.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Let's turn to another weapon which you mentioned which is a three-barrelled gun. That was in fact an anti-aircraft gun, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe it or not, I don't know. We used it during the night to fire tracer bullets into the surrounding woods. We would fire in order to find out if there was anyone over there just in case of an attack. Whether it can take planes down or not, I didn't really know much about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: More questions about that. Firstly, this gun was yellow, wasn't it, in colour?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe it or not, I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Isn't that what you've referred to in a prior statement as the yellow one, moja zuca?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'll skip that question. I'd like to refer you to your 2000 statement to the investigators again, page 1, ERN 00938904, and again you don't need to look at it. I'll just quote and see if you agree. "On October 5, 1992, I was collecting corn in my field with my wife Milenka. At 12.00 p.m. they started shooting from all sides. It was automatic weapon fire, machine-gun fire, and three-barrelled anti-aircraft fire. Shoulder-mounted rockets were fired during the attack." Now, isn't it right when you spoke to investigators of this Tribunal you described that three-barrelled gun as an anti-aircraft gun, or at least one which was shooting anti-aircraft fire?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that it could fire at planes. I don't know now whether it could be used to fire at planes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So that was wrongly recorded in your statement of 2000? That's not something you said?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's right, isn't it, that anti-aircraft guns not meant for firing at human beings, are they then meant for firing at aircraft? We all take that as read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You don't need to answer that question. Move to the next, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Isn't it right that that three-barrelled gun was being used to shoot at people on the 5th of October, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. How should I know what they would have done? I suppose they didn't keep it there for nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You heard it shooting on the day, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that day when the shooting started, it was coming from all sides at the same time. You couldn't really distinguish anything. Everything that was there to be used was used. We didn't really put up any resistance, because if we put up resistance we wouldn't have just gone down like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: But that gun, the three-barrelled gun, was shooting, wasn't it? And that was something you heard.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But also further up from the village - this is something I learned when I returned home - a set of ammunition was found for the Browning gun which belonged to the Muslim forces. For the Browning. And in some cases it may be the same kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. In fact, you know quite a lot about calibres and ammunition and artillery, don't you, Mr. Zikic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Believe it but not. What I said, just to mention something only in those days when I was, I had to know what goes with each of the weapons [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. I'm going to ask you to try and keep your answers a bit shorter and give a yes, no answer if you can, because we do want to conclude as soon as we can. Do you know that the three-barrelled gun was actually a 23-millimetre gun?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You just told us that you needed to know which ammunition went with which weapon. This three-barrelled gun in Fakovici, presumably you were aware of what calibre it took, what calibre of ammunition?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In came maybe a month or two before and the ammunition was not brought; it was kept near the house where it was mounted.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And whose house was that, if you can help us with that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nikolic. If you mean the father's name, in that case, Dragan Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Wasn't that gun captured during the 5th of October, 1992, attack, if you knew that, if you learnt that later?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea what happened after the 5th. It was probably seized. Why would they have left it behind?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I have a new -- actual it's not a new exhibit. It's P527 which I'm going to refer to. And I wonder if a copy could be shown to the witness. I understand it's been given a P number. If it hasn't been tendered --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can't help you there. Only the registrar can give you the information.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I can mention the ERN number of the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm informed by Mr. Siller that we don't have such an exhibit until now.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move on the Prosecution's side. Could you check, please. In other words, it hasn't even been premarked?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If I mentioned the ERN number? Would that assist?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But the problem is the registrar was misled by what we have in the transcript because the transcript said 527. And I can vividly recall you saying 257 and not 527. And then you also gave the ERN number which you can perhaps repeat now.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The original is 03734021 to 03734022. In fact, the English just has an ET suffix afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I apologise to you, Mr. Jones, for the mistake. It is already exhibited -- tendered, yes. Usher, could you please put on the ELMO the English text and give the witness the text in his own language.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'd refer you, Mr. Zikic, just to the second paragraph and I'll read it in English. "In this way we were informed that the attack against these villages started simultaneously, 5 October 1992, at 1200 hours and lasted until 1600 hours. A total of 22 members of the Serbian army were killed while the enemy had around 40 dead. On this occasion the enemy burnt down several family houses and the old school in Fakovici and took away a three-barrel M-55 anti-aircraft gun and a four-barrel 382-millimetre MB mortar, one of which was not working; three or four Zoljas, 64-millimetre MAT hand-held rocket launcher; one M84 PM light machine-gun; ten AP automatic rifle; a number of hand grenades; and 1500 7.62-millimetre bullets. And according to another source, in addition to the above stated, two tractors of ammunition." Now, Mr. Zikic, you've told us you were issuing weapons and ammunition from May 1992 until I think you said July or August. I'd like to go through this list and see if you're familiar with some of these items and whether you can confirm that they were weapons which you're aware of as being in Fakovici on the day of the attack. We dealt with the three-barrel anti-aircraft gun. Are four-barrel gun, are you aware of a four-barrel gun in Fakovici?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For as long as I was at that storage where the weapons were being kept, they had that three-barrel weapon that I told you about that was mounted on a truck. As for the remaining weapons, I've already told you everything I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. In that case I won't go through the list, and there's no need to tender this; it's already an exhibit. But if that is right, Mr. Zikic, that list of weaponry, that's a lot of weaponry for a small town, isn't it? Is it possible that -- let me rephrase that. You accept, don't you, there was possibly that much weaponry in Fakovici on the 5th of October, 1992, what we've seen on the list?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I find that incredible. I do have a remark to make, however. You say 22 soldiers were killed. A total number of soldiers killed in the area on that day would be 23, and I can read it out to you if you like. These are soldiers and where the women, too, could be soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's all right. That's not necessary. You say you confirm that 23 soldiers died. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. On that day, the general attack that was carried out, 25 inhabitants were killed. And soldiers. A total of 25 persons. There's there's a list name by name; I have it here. If women, too, are to be considered soldiers. Well, anyone can say whatever they like.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, on your definition, Mr. Zikic, surely if a woman picked up a weapon and started shooting, she would be a soldier?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Moving on from that subject.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But this never happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Mr. Zikic, you were arrested in the early stages of the attack, weren't you? So you didn't see everything that happened on that day.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was arrested --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... we've heard your story. We don't need to revisit it. Zoljas you've referred to in your testimony. It's right, isn't it, that a Zolja can set fire to a building pretty easily?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I -- well, I can't answer the question whether it can set fire to anything or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Didn't you tell us that the guardhouse was hit by a Zolja, that it went up in flames as a result?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that it burned down the house. The greatest number of victims was in that house, I think six. And they were so burned down to the extent that you couldn't identify any of them. There was just ashes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That guardhouse, is that the one you said was reinforced? You described the guardhouse as being reinforced -- sorry, if you could give me a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I can certainly pause there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: This is a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will have a minutes break starting from now.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, over the break I reviewed the remaining questions which I had and in the interests of finishing with this witness today, a witness who's probably very tired after two days, I can certainly be finished within 15 to 20 minutes. I understand that you're not putting any pressure on me to finish, but I would certainly try to conclude --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There's definitely no pressure on you. I am to imagine that we are to expect a re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, a very brief one at that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's perfect. So let's get cracking.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Mr. Zikic, just a few more questions after the 5th of October, 1992. Isn't it right that on that day there were hundreds of civilians, men, women, and children, all in your village running around, grabbing food? That sort of thing?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is true. The numbers were even greater, judging by what was taken from the village on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Would you even say thousands? Could there have been thousands of people?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything that was taken away from those villages, that certainly -- that amount of things would have taken a great many people because our people returned the next day to the villages and everything had been taken away. I don't mean sofas and stuff like that. All the valuables, all food and wheat. It would have taken a great many people to simply carry all those things off.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You saw some of that on the day. Wasn't it a scene of absolute chaos with these women, children, civilians, and people in uniforms as well all there in the space of your village? Would you accept that it was a chaotic scene? That's all I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think a civilised nation may find it very difficult to understand what I'm telling you. In addition to shooting people were banging on some cans and they were killing dogs. It was seething from all sides, all over the place. There was a lot of noise, and God knows what was being done. I don't think this is something you would find easy to understand, coming from a civilised nation as you are.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Mr. Zikic, isn't it right that with all these people and all this going on, these people were completely out of control?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is my opinion that it was indeed out of control. Someone had to know about this, obviously, but it's difficult to speak about these things now, whether had control over what was happening or not. It's impossible for me to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The banging of pots. Was that women and children banging on pots to make a great deal of noise? Is that what it was?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was probably the civilian population, as they were seizing livestock just in case there was anyone nearing to make it easier for them to collect in livestock.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You told us they took livestock. I believe you mentioned that wheat was taken from your brother. Isn't it right that these people were desperate for food?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand that fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why else would they, for example, be taking a horse away in case they didn't need that?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And you even mentioned I think that people were chasing chickens and you thought it extraordinary that they could catch a chicken. It's right, isn't it, that if you were trying to control those people it's pretty hard to catch someone who is chasing a chicken, pretty hard to control these people?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the chickens that were caught, it took a great number of civilians. It would have been impossible because the next morning -- well, not me personally, but those who survived and crossed the Drina River, there was not a single chicken left in any of the villages. They had all been released. If they had been pent up, well okay. But there was not chicken to be seen anywhere around for miles. Therefore, there were probably many people doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: My point is this, Mr. Zikic, in one of the statements we've seen you've said the people in uniform didn't try to control the civilians. But what I'm putting to you in this scene of absolute pandemonium, this scene of people running around, grabbing chickens, no one, no army could stop them from doing what they wanted to do to get food. Is that something you accept? Is that what you accept?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, moving to the burning of houses, you didn't actually any houses being set on fire -- by that I mean a person putting a house to a flame on the 5th of October, 1992, did you? You saw smoke and you saw buildings on fire but you never saw a person setting fire to a house?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, except Akif told me that God had set fire to my house. That's when I was in prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I was really asking what you saw with your own eyes. You don't know, do you, whether some -- whether -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You don't know either, do you, whether some of the damage which you later saw in Fakovici to houses was caused by missiles, bombs, or Zoljas rather than -- because of being set on fire?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything -- I was wondering to myself, how was it possible to set so many things on fire at the same time along a distance of 8, 10, or 12 kilometres, all these villages burning at the same time. This could not have been done by a weapon. There must have been some flammable fluid that was used or something. I'm not going into that because I simply don't know, but I don't think it was done by a weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Let's look at what you've said about all the villages being set on fire at the same time. You're not including the Muslim villages Zanjevo, Voljevica and those other villages in that description, are you? Because they were not destroyed on that day, were they?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As I said, in the month of June Zanjevo was evacuated because they received word that they should evacuate a long time earlier. I don't know about Voljevica. That was not in my area. I'm talking about Zanjevo. There was nothing there burning on that day because they had left before that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's not because they left, is it? Isn't it right that it's because the Serbs had burnt the houses in Zanjevo back in June after the people were expelled? So those houses were already burnt?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Isn't it also right that on that day, the 5th of October, 1992, there was a massive barrage of artillery from the other side of the Drina, from the Serb side, as a counterattack against the Muslim attack? Is that something you're aware of?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This didn't happen. They left Skelani but they couldn't cross from Bosnia. They headed down the right-hand side riverbank of the Drina River. And when it was all over, they started.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm no talking about not necessarily Bosnian Serb forces, but artillery on the other side of the Drina in Serbia, that they were shooting grenades on the 5th of October to try and repel the Muslim forces or the attacking forces. Is that something you either saw or heard of at some later stage?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand. I did hear about it later while I was in Serbia. There was no shooting. We left at 1600 hours all together from Fakovici with the army, and what do I know? Up until that point, nothing had happened. Later I found out when the men in Skelani were told, were informed, they tried to head towards us through Bosnia but they were not allowed or they simply couldn't, so they took the Serbian side of the river. And there they used mortars to fire a number of missiles. I'm not sure how many. But I was quite far away from Fakovici when I was told something along the lines of, These Chetniks of yours are late, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And those men from Skelani, that would be VRS, Bosnian Serb army forces?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Just three more questions or four more. Yesterday you went through methodically saying which house was destroyed first and then second. At best that wasn't something you saw with your own eyes; that was something you were told afterwards?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Something that I was watching from below the bank of the River Drina and I was watching my own house burning. I saw this with my own eyes; the distance is perhaps 300 to 400 metres. I was close to the centre of Fakovici because that's where my house is, in the very centre of Fakovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you see Dragan Nikolic's house, the house where you said the three-barrelled gun was stationed? Did you see that as one of the houses which went up -- which was destroyed?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, I've already said that I was near that house. The distance was maybe about 100 metres. The cottage that I referred to, I said whose, and this was perhaps 100 metres from that house. It wasn't burning when I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'll stop you there for a moment. You mentioned that you were there at the house. Did you at any time yourself shoot the three-barrelled gun which you referred to earlier at the people who were attacking?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You don't have to believe me, but I was issued with an M-48 and I never fired a single bullet nor would I ever do so. I'm the kind of man who doesn't -- it's not so easy to shoot a man. At least that's what I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, this was the first -- correct me if I'm wrong, this was the first action which you had seen where your village was attacked, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first action that I saw was that one, but every third or fourth night there were attempts from the woods and you could hear shooting from there. Because all the Serbian villages before Fakovici were burned. Fakovici was the only one that was not burned on the day that I was captured.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's just that yesterday you described that you knew the tactics, speaking of the Muslims. But isn't it right that those tactics you described, expelling people, burning their homes, are the tactics which you saw the SDS and Serbs adopt in Zanjevo when they expelled Muslims from their homes?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't say that because before that -- I don't know when, but a month before that Ratkovici, Ducici, Dvorista, Bradjevina, and I can't remember all the villages, were burned. This was perhaps a month before that. And as soon as that was done --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's not something you saw, did you? You weren't present in Ratkovici or Bradjevina, were you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could see some of the villages when they were burning because those that are closer -- but you could see such as Vesici. I didn't mention all of them. Maybe ones that are half a kilometre to a kilometre away as the crow flies up in Brdo. Then when you come back to the village, there wasn't a single Muslim left.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We won't deal with Ratkovici or Bradjevina. I want to ask you one final question to clarify something that appeared to have been said yesterday. It appeared in the transcript that the church in Fakovici was destroyed, but that's not right, is it? The church wasn't destroyed, it was the vicarage or the parish building where the priests lived. Is that right? The church wasn't destroyed?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's true that the church did not burn down. They only broke the door down and entered and wrote down, We will come back, signed Alija, which doesn't necessarily mean this was Alija Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: One final question. The school which you referred to earlier as being a storage space where weapons and ammunition was stored, was that damaged?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The glass wasn't even shattered on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Jones. Re-examination, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mr. Zikic, you testified previously on direct and you were asked on cross about seeing Naser Oric or talking to him during your time that you were imprisoned in Srebrenica. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that and I remember it well.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And the person who came to you and said his name was Naser Oric, did this person come -- was it the same person that came to you the four times while you were in prison in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is the same person.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And did anyone else other than that individual come to you and claim to be Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what the prisoners knew, those who came to the prison before I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Okay. But my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think that is an answer to your question. It may be a question of interpretation. Could you repeat your question again, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes indeed I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did anyone else, any other person, come to you and say to you that I am Naser Oric? Other than the person you saw the four times, did anyone else come to you and say I am Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stated that he said I am Naser Oric. When the first visit took place, we were sitting on the floor because we all had difficulties in standing up. One of the prisoners said, Hurry-up, Naser is coming in. They knew him from before.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. When you met Akif, when Akif came to visit, did he say he was Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know Akif, so he couldn't say that he was him.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. And when you were interrogated or questioned by this Mirzat, did that person say to you that he was Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And when you were interviewed in the -- by the police during one of the times that you were questioned, did at that time while they were questioning you say that they were Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, as the postmaster or manager of the Fakovici post office. This is a very public position. As you were in the public eye -- I guess what I'm trying to ask is you were known? A lot of people knew you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. I think that more people knew me than the president of the Bratunac municipality. The people liked me, both Muslims and Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And in fact one of the guards in the prison also knew you prior to your being kept prisoner there.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He knew me. He was a former police officer from Bratunac. His nickname was Cude. His last name was Omerovic and his first name was Sabahudin.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, you were asked a series of questions from the statement you gave in 1994, and I'm not going to show you the statement again at this time. But my question to you is: You had an opportunity to read this statement. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. Well, let me just ask you in this statement that I'm reading from and I think it was entered into evidence by the Defence. I don't have the Defence number at this time, but the statement ERN --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: D135. Let's move, Ms. Richardson, because we have questions as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: You say in this statement you noticed two black -- two blacks between the soldiers and one of them approached you, lifted you, and put a knife to your throat. Now, did this incident involve one person who you term as a black person or did it involve two?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I always said that when I was captured one black man ran towards me with a knife.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. So if it says two in this statement, this is not -- this is inaccurate. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not true that they were -- there were two. There was one, and that is what I've always said and I stand by that. I cannot say there were two when there was only one. If you allow me to say something more about that question. I wouldn't be sure unless some of the soldiers asked me as we were on the road, Do you know, Chetnik, what jihad is? And I said, I don't know. Do you know what mujahedin are? I said, I don't know. Well, that's what you saw and then you will see when they start severing Serbian heads. They didn't say "cutting," but severing Serbian heads. So that's how I got to that conclusion when they said, you will see. That's how I came to the conclusion that it was someone from the outside. It didn't state on his forehead, but I don't want to claim now if he was a mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's not open new chapters.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you If you can keep your answers as brief as possible; we're running short on time. Now, with respect to your statement in 1994 it also says that you stated that during the interrogation that Naser Oric would visit the room. Is that true? Or did he only visit the other four times?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but he only talked to us through the bars. I can't remember what you call them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: But he was not present during the interrogation?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right --

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On either of the occasions, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: So if it says that in your statement, this is also inaccurate?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: When you repeat or you put a second question like this, you confuse -- automatically you confuse the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll just withdraw that question, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The moment he denied the presence of Naser Oric in the course of both interrogations, because he mentioned two, that's it, you have your answer. You don't need to put the question again.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Point taken, Your Honour. I'll move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: You also testified that Zoran Brankovic was smashed during the exchange or when he was taken off the truck, you said by three to four people. Could you tell us, were those people were civilian or military clothing?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were wearing military clothing, and this was done in front of the truck, so I could see that with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And you said that your arm was injured during that period of time as well by Beli. Is this Beli the same person who would beat you while you were in the prison?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the same Beli. I don't know his name, but there is a village Pale near Srebrenica and I found out that he's from Pale. But please don't confuse that with the Pale near Sarajevo. This is Pale near Srebrenica that I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, you were asked about the injuries you received, whether they were prior to your being in the prison or did they occur before. And you previously testified that you were beaten during the time that you were in prison.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you have asked this about my arm but I have already forgotten about that a little bit. That was Beli's last farewell to me because they stopped the truck and he had to say something once he had stopped the truck. He climbed up on to the tire and struck me on the right shoulder and said, Chetnik, this is my last farewell to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And your teeth -- when you were struck in the mouth with a rifle, were you in the prison at that time and your teeth were knocked out?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm not sure about that evidence and if my learned friend can refer us to the transcript so we can check if that's an accurate statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: First he stated they were knocked out and then he corrected himself and said they were actually broken. When did that happen? Did it happen while you were still in the cell or did it happen after you were in prison or after you had been taken out of the prison cell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I never said that when I was at -- having my interrogation with Mirzat. There was a soldier standing at the door on the way out with a rifle placed across his shoulders. Then he turned around and with the barrel suddenly hit me. And that's when the -- I lost three or four teeth. One fell out; the rest were broken. One was knocked out when I was captured, when I was being tied. But I'm not sure exactly when it was knocked out.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: With respect to your -- with respect to your visit to the doctor after you were exchanged, prior to visiting the doctor, and we had an exhibit of your medical report, prior to that visit which was about three days later, you testified, did you see a doctor or did a doctor examine you immediately after you were released? The same day.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was supposed to go to the hospital to have a chest x-ray, so that's all that there is. I was supposed to report back on the 21st; I didn't go. I told you that some woman told me about these sheepskins and that's how it all ended, I'm talking about the sheepskins. That is the actually the sum total of my treatment.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did you -- all right. Well, if you would permit me to ask, Your Honour, I do need to lead a little bit on this with respect to a particular visit I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead, if you are, and we'll see what comes out of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did you -- were you examined by a doctor in Bratunac, a Veljko, and then given papers to go to the hospital for treatment? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Veljko was a doctor. After I had a bath I went there and Dr. Veljko was there and he gave me something for my pain because my wife and sister-in-law were waiting already waiting for me to travel to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And what day was that? Was that the same day you were released?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I spent the night at my wife's sister in Bratunac. I said that already. I had a bath there, I spent the night there. So the next day I went towards Lazarevac. Once I got to Lazarevac, I didn't go. My son actually wanted me to go right away, but I was too weak and because of my eyes. He wanted me to go. He asked me to go but I didn't. So I actually went to see the doctor on the 19th. I knew myself that a doctor really couldn't do much for me.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. Now, with respect to the women in Fakovici, were they given weapons to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Men over 50 didn't have any kind of obligation, and that is why it was easy for me also to be relieved of my duty at the depot. And women also.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: You were also asked about a guardhouse and I think you -- I believe you testified that six people died in that house. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do and ...

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Okay. If you would just answer with a yes and then I'll ask the other part of the question. When did you learn what happened -- or did there come a time when you learned what happened to that guardhouse and how it was incinerated?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found out only once I left the prison.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: While you were in the prison, was it ever discussed or did you hear anyone discussing the destruction of the guardhouse?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
